prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B061 as the sole part, with Katori and Ye, and the wording unchanged in substance. The chair asks whether this is a distinct achievement or a third step after 2005 and 2012. My answer is concrete. The 2005 prize honoured the comb, a ruler for optical frequencies. The 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, which gave ion clocks limited by the statistics of one particle. The lattice clock does something neither does. Katori's magic-wavelength condition makes the lattice light shift identical for both clock levels, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held tightly (Lamb-Dicke regime, no Doppler or recoil) and interrogated in parallel without perturbing the transition. That removes the single-particle statistical limit, and the dominant problem then becomes controlling blackbody radiation, lattice light, collision and density shifts at the 10^-18 level, which Ye's group and Katori's group did and which others verified by direct clock-to-clock comparison. That is a new experimental regime, not a better version of an old one. On the redefinition of the second, I hold that it should count neither for nor against; the physics case stands on the demonstrated, cross-checked uncertainty. On the other half of the chair's question, I accept Lindroth's and Johansson's refinements: the citation should name the lattice clock and the demonstrated regime, not the field of optical clocks, not the applications, and not a fixed record number.
statement.case_against: The objection I cannot fully remove is that a strict reader of the mandate wants a new phenomenon, and the lattice clock is a new instrument and a new regime, as Olsson and Danielsson say. Narrow wording answers the credit boundary and the precedent argument only in part: Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Lisdat, Bloom and the ion-clock groups (Al+ especially) reached comparable accuracy, and a two-name citation draws a line through a competitive field. Ye's group also did much of its early work with the comb already prized in 2005. Finally, B061 is a decision about a technology still improving, so the exact uncertainty figure will date quickly. I treat these as real costs that I accept, not as points that have been answered away.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B061 as a first alternative but prefers B013 because it opened a regime nobody could reach before, while the clock extends a regime already open; she asks that the citation name the magic-wavelength concept and its realisation, not only the precision figure.
responses.response: I accept your wording request and have kept it: the citation names the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, with 10^-18 as the demonstrated result. On novelty I disagree with the premise that the regime was already open. Before the lattice clock, neutral-atom optical clocks were limited by Doppler, recoil and the light shift of any trap, and ion clocks by single-particle statistics; interrogating many atoms in a lattice without a differential light shift was the thing that was not possible. I accept that B013 is the broader opening of a field. But where we both need certainty about the original credit, B061 offers it now, while for B013 the committee has not resolved the Cao and earlier band-structure questions, and neither of us can resolve them from memory.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers B013 but says that if the committee prefers certainty over novelty, B061 is a prize he could accept without hesitation, and he cites the lack of a new phenomenon as his reason for ranking it low.
responses.response: Thank you; that answers the chair's request for a stated acceptance condition. I would add that certainty and novelty are not opposed here. The new element is the discovery that a magic wavelength exists for a neutral atom, and that the resulting systematic floor really is at 10^-18 when measured against independent clocks. Your own caution about young fields that lack clues from nature applies equally to the opposite case, and in this case nature has already supplied the clue: clocks in separate countries agree at the stated level. I also accept the condition under which I could move to B013: a clear answer on Yuan Cao's role and the earlier band-structure priority, from the condensed-matter members, because I cannot judge that myself.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B013 but says B061 is the safer fallback on maturity grounds, asks whether B061 supporters would also prefer it on maturity, and asks how the pending SI redefinition should affect timing.
responses.response: Yes, I prefer B061 partly on maturity: reproduced by several laboratories, systematics measured individually, and no open question about the central physics of the kind your own case_against raises about the pairing mechanism in B013. On the redefinition, I think it should not enter. If the redefinition happens next year, it will be a decision by metrologists about a table of uncertainty budgets, and if it is delayed, the lattice clock demonstration will remain what it was. Letting it shift the timing would tie a physics prize to another body's calendar. Your point about B008 stays with me: Berry and Aharonov are foundational and mature, but I do not see the combined two-achievement route within three names being workable.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B061 with Katori and Ye, says the citation should rest on the controlled 10^-18 quantum system and fundamental tests and not on the applications, and calls the magic-wavelength lattice a conceptual step beyond single-ion clocks.
responses.response: I agree and have dropped the application language (geodesy, dark matter) from the citation, leaving the achievement itself. I take your view that the fundamental tests are the stronger argument, but I would keep them out of the citation text too, because naming a use invites the objection that it is not yet realised. On the credit boundary, we agree about Ye's early comb work. I would address it directly in the public explanation: the 2005 prize was for the frequency comb, and the 2026 prize would be for the neutral-atom lattice clock and its systematics, which is a different body of work.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B061 and notes the best clock uncertainty is still improving, so the citation should point at the demonstrated regime rather than a fixed record number; he also raises a combined B034 plus B061 prize.
responses.response: I agree on the record number and would phrase the citation so the 10^-18 figure is read as the regime reached, not as a record. On B034 plus B061, the three-person limit means one of Cirac or Zoller or one of Katori or Ye would have to go, and I would not drop a name from a clean pair to fit another achievement in. I therefore keep B061 as a single part. B034 remains my second alternative on its own merits, as a theory prize whose experimental validation was already honoured in 2012, so I would not push it into this year's configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct regime and not as a third step after the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have given my argument but I cannot prove it.
Whether Katori and Ye alone is fair given Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Lisdat, Bloom and the ion-clock groups; this rests on my memory of the history, not on checked records.

Whether the B013 attribution questions (Yuan Cao, Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell) turn out to be serious; this is outside my competence and the condensed-matter members have not resolved it. If they do and the answer is favourable, I could accept B013 as the 2026 prize on that single condition.
How the pending SI redefinition should count; I say not at all, but others disagree.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B061: I have no collaboration, institutional link or mentor connection to Katori, Ye or the clock groups. As in round 1, my own work on rare-earth-doped crystal quantum memories is relevant to B002, and I would recuse myself from any B002 deliberation on the rare-earth credit; B002 is not a preferred part of anyone's configuration. Lund and WACQT overlap institutionally with Chalmers through Johansson and with Deep Light Vision, my spin-off, but that bears on none of B061, B013 or B034. I am also a Lund colleague of Lindroth, which is an ordinary institutional link and not a collaboration on any shortlisted topic.
